raw_text:
CARPAL TUNNEL SYNDROME (CTS)

Age

30–60 years (Common CTS group)

<30 years (Consider overuse or other neuropathy)



Where is the pain located ?

Palmar wrist/hand (Median nerve distribution → CTS)

Dorsal wrist (Suggests other pathology)



Symptoms distribution

Thumb, index, middle, and radial half of ring finger (CLASSIC CTS)

Whole hand (Consider proximal nerve or systemic issue)



How did the symptoms begin ?

Gradual (Typical CTS)

Sudden (Consider trauma)



What is the pain type?

Tingling, numbness, burning (Neuropathic → CTS)

Sharp localized pain (Musculoskeletal)



Do you experience night symptoms?

Yes (VERY STRONG CTS INDICATOR)

No



Do symptoms wake you from sleep?

Yes (Classic CTS)

No



Do you shake your hand to relieve symptoms?

Yes (“Flick sign” → HIGHLY SPECIFIC CTS)

No



What aggravates the pain

Repetitive wrist use (Typing, gripping) (CTS)

Impact/trauma (Consider injury)



Is there weakness (grip or thumb)?

Yes (Thenar involvement → advanced CTS)

No



Does pain radiate above the wrist?

Yes (Possible proximal nerve involvement)

No (Supports CTS)



Objective / Observation

Is there thenar muscle wasting?

Yes (Chronic CTS)

No



Is there reduced sensation in median nerve distribution?

Yes (CTS)

No



Is there weak thumb opposition?

Yes (Median nerve motor deficit)

No



Red Flag

Severe progressive weakness?

Yes (Urgent referral)

No



Symptoms involving entire arm?

Yes (Cervical pathology)

No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

Phalen’s Test

Patient flexes wrists fully and holds position.

Sign is positive if numbness/tingling occurs.

If positive, indicates CTS.



Tinel’s Sign

Examiner taps over carpal tunnel.

Sign is positive if tingling in median nerve distribution.

If positive, indicates CTS.



Carpal Compression Test

Examiner applies direct pressure over carpal tunnel.

Sign is positive if symptoms are reproduced.

     If positive, indicates CTS.





DE QUERVAIN’S TENOSYNOVITIS

Age

30–50 years (Common group)

Any age (With repetitive use)



Where is the pain located?

Radial wrist (Thumb side) (KEY SIGN)

Ulnar wrist (Other pathology)



How did the pain begin?

Gradual (Overuse)

Sudden (Less common)



What aggravates the pain?

Thumb movement/gripping (CLASSIC)

Wrist extension (Less specific)

Is there pain with lifting objects (e.g., child, kettle)?

Yes (Very typical)

No



Is there swelling near thumb base?

Yes (Inflammation of tendon sheath)

No



Do you feel creaking sensation?

Yes (Tenosynovitis)

No



Objective / Observation

Is there ttenderness over radial styloid?

Yes (PRIMARY FINDING)

No



Is there pain with resisted thumb extension/abduction?

Yes (Abductor Pollicis Longus (APL) and Extensor Pollicis Brevis (EPB) involvement)

No



Red Flag

History of trauma?

a. Yes (Rule out fracture)

b. No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

Finkelstein’s Test

Patient makes a fist with thumb inside fingers. Examiner ulnar deviates wrist.

Sign is positive if sharp pain at radial wrist.

If positive, indicates De Quervain’s.



WHAT Test (Wrist Hyperflexion Abduction of Thumb)

Patient hyperflexes wrist and abducts thumb against resistance.

Sign is positive if pain is reproduced.

If positive, indicates De Quervain’s.





 WRIST SPRAIN (LIGAMENTOUS INJURY)

Age



Where is the pain located ?

Localized to wrist (Depends on ligament)

Diffuse (Less specific)



Is there any history of trauma?

Yes (PRIMARY DIAGNOSTIC DRIVER)

No

What is the mechanism of injury

Fall on outstretched hand (FOOSH) (Classic)

No trauma (Consider other conditions)



How did the pain begin?

Sudden (Injury)

Gradual (Not sprain)



Pain type

Sharp initially, then aching

Burning/tingling (Neurological)



Is swelling present?

Yes (Acute injury)

No



Is the pain aggravated by movement?

Yes (Ligament involvement)

No



Objective / Observation

Is there swelling/bruising?

Yes (Acute sprain)

No



Does the patient experience pain with ligament stress?

Yes (Confirms sprain)

No



Is ROM reduced?

Yes (Protective limitation)

No



Red Flag

Is there severe pain with deformity?

Yes (Fracture/dislocation)

No



Is the patient unable to move the wrist?

Yes (Serious injury)

No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

1. Ligament Stress Tests

a. Examiner applies stress to specific ligaments.

b. Sign is positive if pain/laxity occurs.

If positive, indicates ligament injury.







 TFCC INJURY (Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex)

Age

20–50 years (Common group)

Older (Degenerative tears possible)



Where is the pain located ?

Ulnar side of wrist (KEY SIGN)

Radial side (Other pathology)



Is there any history of trauma?

Yes (FOOSH or twisting)

No (Degenerative)



What aggravates the pain?

Ulnar deviation or rotation (CLASSIC)

Grip only (Less specific)



Do you experience pain when clicking or catching?

Yes (Mechanical → TFCC)

No



Is there weak grip strength?

Yes (Common finding)

No



Objective / Observation

Is there tenderness over ulnar wrist?

Yes (Primary finding)

No



Is there pain with pronation/supination?

Yes (TFCC involvement)

No



Red Flag



Severe instability?

a. Yes (Serious ligament injury)

b. No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

TFCC Load Test

Wrist in ulnar deviation + axial load + rotation

Positive if pain/clicking occurs

If positive, indicates TFCC injury.



Press Test

Patient pushes up from chair using hands

Positive if ulnar wrist pain

If positive, suggests TFCC tear.

GANGLION CYST



1.         Age

15–40 years (Common group)

Any age



2.	Where is the pain located?

Dorsal wrist (Most common site)

Volar wrist (Also possible)



3.	Do you notice a swelling/lump?

Yes (DEFINING FEATURE → ganglion cyst)

No



4.	How did the swelling begin?

Gradual (Typical)

Sudden (Less common)



5.	Pain type

Mild ache or painless (Common)

Severe pain (Consider other pathology)



6.	Does the size of the lump change?

Yes (Characteristic of ganglion cyst)

No



7.	What aggravates the pain ?

Wrist movement or loading (Supports cyst)

No change



8.	Is there any history of trauma?

Yes (May contribute)

No



Objective / Observation

Is there visible or palpable cystic swelling?

Yes (PRIMARY SIGN)

No



Is transillumination positive?

Yes (Fluid-filled → ganglion)

No



Is there tenderness over cyst?

Yes

No



Red Flag

Hard, immobile mass?

Yes (Possible tumor → refer)

No



Rapid unexplained growth?

Yes (Investigate)

No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

Transillumination Test

a. Light is applied through the swelling

b. Positive if light passes through

If positive, indicates fluid-filled cyst (ganglion).





INTERSECTION SYNDROME

Age

20–50 years (Active individuals)

Any age



Where is the pain located?

Dorsal radial forearm (4–6 cm proximal to wrist) (KEY SIGN)

Radial styloid (Suggests De Quervain’s)



How did the pain begin?

Gradual (Overuse)

Sudden (Less common)



What aggravates the pain?

Repetitive wrist extension (Rowing, lifting) (CLASSIC)

Thumb movement only (De Quervain’s)



Do you feel creaking or squeaking?

Yes (Characteristic crepitus → intersection syndrome)

No



Is there swelling?

Yes (Inflammatory)

No



Objective / Observation

Is there tenderness proximal to radial styloid?

Yes (Differentiates from De Quervain’s)

No



Is there crepitus with wrist movement?

Yes (KEY FINDING)

No



Is there pain with resisted wrist extension?

Yes

No

Red Flag

History of trauma?

a. Yes (Rule out fracture)

b. No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

Resisted Wrist Extension Test

a. Patient extends wrist against resistance

b. Positive if pain/crepitus occurs

If positive, indicates intersection syndrome.





SCAPHOID FRACTURE (CRITICAL RED FLAG)

Age

15–40 years (Common group)

Any age (With trauma)



Where is the pain located?

Radial wrist/anatomical snuffbox (KEY SIGN)

Diffuse wrist pain



Is there any history of trauma?

Yes (FOOSH) (PRIMARY DIAGNOSTIC DRIVER)

No



How did the pain begin?

Immediate after fall (Fracture)

Gradual (Not fracture)



What aggravates the pan ?

Wrist movement/gripping

No change



Is swelling present?

Yes (May be mild)

No



Did you ignore the injury initially?

Yes (Common in scaphoid fractures)

No



Objective / Observation

Is there tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox?

Yes (MOST IMPORTANT SIGN)

No



Is there pain with axial thumb compression?

Yes (Scaphoid injury)

No



Is the grip strength reduced?

Yes

No



Red Flag (CRITICAL)

Do you experience persistent pain after fall despite normal X-ray?

Yes (Treat as fracture)

No



Delayed presentation?

Yes (Risk of non-union/AVN)

No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS

Snuffbox Tenderness Test

Palpation of anatomical snuffbox

Positive if pain present

If positive, indicates scaphoid fracture.



Scaphoid Compression Test

Axial load applied through thumb

Positive if pain occurs

If positive, suggests scaphoid fracture.





KIENBÖCK’S DISEASE (AVN OF LUNATE)

Age

20–40 years (Common group)

>50 years (Less common)



Where is the pain located?

Dorsal central wrist (KEY SIGN)

Radial/ulnar wrist (Other pathology)



How did the pain begin?

Gradual (AVN pattern)

Sudden (Consider trauma)



How will you describe the pain?

Deep, aching (AVN)

Sharp (Other pathology)



What aggravates the pain

Wrist loading/activity

Rest



Do you experience pain at rest or night?

Yes (Red flag → AVN)

No



Is there any history of repetitive trauma or loading?

Yes (Risk factor)

No



Objective / Observation

Is there tenderness over lunate (central dorsal wrist)?

Yes (PRIMARY FINDING)

No



Is the wrist ROM reduced?

Yes (Progressive stiffness)

No



Is the grip strength weak?

Yes

No



Red Flag



Do you experience progressive stiffness and pain?

Yes (AVN progression)

No



Do you experience night pain not relieved by rest?

Yes (Serious pathology)

No



SPECIAL CONFIRMATORY TESTS 

No single definitive clinical test



Axial Load Test

a. Apply compression through wrist

b. Positive if central wrist pain

If positive, suggests intra-articular pathology (Kienböck’s possible)
